Chapter Thirteen: Lucía’s
Archive
Lucía did not begin with Malinche.
She began with Ofelia, who had
spent fourteen years asking for a
correction to her daughter's name.
The error had travelled from a
report into later files and
newspaper accounts. Ofelia had
travelled after it with copies, bus
tickets, and the name her daughter
used at home.
The new archive occupied a
borrowed classroom in Amealco.
Eleven people, four boxes, two
unreliable laptops, and a thermos
of coffee filled it without quite
making it an institution. A window
faced a wall on which someone had
painted a woman holding a book
and a torch. Her face borrowed
features from several public
figures. Nobody present knew who
had painted her; everyone had an
opinion about the torch near the
paper.
Q's approved visits now included
the classroom. He had agreed to
help compare deposit terms and
public references. Lucía gave him
the work list and pointed to the
only chair without a box on it.
“That one is yours until the kettle
boils. Then we need the socket
behind it.”
He put his bag beneath it. “I've had
less secure appointments.”
Ofelia wanted the school notebook
compared with two official
versions. The retained folder in
Tijuana had another copy, but she
had brought her own documents.
They were not dependent on its
return to begin this piece of work.
Q put the sources in separate
columns and read the spellings
back. Ofelia corrected one letter he
had taken for a flourish.
“She made her capitals like that,”
Ofelia said. “She said mine looked
as if they had been frightened.”
Q asked to see the comparison.
Ofelia wrote her own initial on
scrap paper, then her daughter's.
He could see the difference. She
laughed before folding the scrap
into the notebook.
She turned to another page to
show him what the teacher had
written about both their hands. Q
moved the official copies aside to
make room.
Other tables held materials about
the women institutions had made
into national symbols. The
Malinche file brought together
textbooks, translations, film
scenes, and arguments about how
a translator became a convenient
place to deposit blame. The Sor

plates.facing_text:
Juana file included poems and
competing readings, not an
instruction that the poet's own
formidable arguments should
disappear beneath a new account
of her silence. The Guadalupe
materials included devotional
images, family stories, political
uses, and objections to putting all
those things under one heading.
“Not the same kind of subject,” Q
said when Lucía asked him to
check the working categories.
“Historical people, a religious
image, and the lives built around
its uses. One label would make the
differences look like missing
details.”
“Can the catalog keep the
arguments beside the
arrangement?”
“Yes. If we record who made each
connection and don't turn every
connection into a public link.”
They tested a small register on the
materials whose terms permitted
it. Some connections stayed
private. Some items were not ready
for entry. The arrangement could
be questioned without requiring
every participant to assemble the
whole collection again from
memory.
That evening Rebeca arrived with
marked scripts and a notebook.
She had played a revolutionary
heroine in a series produced by a
Castalia subsidiary. In the second
season a synthetic performer had
taken over the role, including
several gestures Rebeca said she
had developed in rehearsal.
“They kept the voice and removed
the arguments,” she said.
Q asked what she wanted help
establishing. Rebeca opened the
notebook at a scene about a
woman waiting for a train. The
printed script made her apologize
for being late. Rebeca's version
asked the man why he had
assumed she meant to leave with
him.
“They used that line,” she said.
“Then called the revision
improvised texture when I asked
about payment.”
She permitted Q to read those
pages with her. Between them lay
grocery lists and notes about a
man who had confused difficulty
with asking what work included. Q
kept no scan. Rebeca wanted to
retain the original and decide later
which passages could support a
claim.
“That line changes the whole
scene,” he said.

plates.facing_text:
“It also makes the next line sound
stupid.”
He read the next line. It did. They
spent ten minutes making fun of
an actor who had been directed to
look noble while demanding an
explanation the woman no longer
owed him. Rebeca did the look. Q
attempted it with his damaged
shoulder and produced something
she called a disappointed
municipal clock.
“May I use that?” he asked.
“The look?”
“The clock. In the book.”
“Yes. Don't improve it.”
When they returned to the
contribution list, Q could identify
the revised lines without claiming
that every bodily decision in a
performance could be returned in
a document. Rebeca wanted
particular acknowledgments and
payment questions answered, not a
certificate declaring her the sole
author of the weather in the scene.
Two donors visited the next
afternoon. Mariela ran a printing
business in San Juan del Río and
brought a pencil that she
sharpened over an old envelope.
The other donor put his phone
beside the budget before asking
whether the archive would provide
a machine demonstration. Lucía
had mentioned that Q would be
working there, knowing it helped
secure the meeting, but had not
told him that his presence was part
of the attraction.
“I can explain the work I'm doing,”
he said. “I didn't agree to an
appearance. Lucía, is that what
was offered?”
She said she had offered his
presence, not a performance.
Hearing the distinction aloud did
not improve it.
“I should have asked you.”
In the corridor Lucía showed him
the unanswered messages that had
preceded the invitation. His name
appeared in the one that had
received a reply.
“I wanted to get them through the
door,” she said.
“So did I. I'd probably have said
yes.”
“I thought you would.”
“I'd like to be there for that part.”
She put the phone away.
“Twenty minutes on the work,” he
said. “No recording or personal
endorsement. Then I have a call
I've promised not to move.”
“With the Custodian?”

“He has discovered a paragraph he
can shorten. I don't want him left
alone with it.”
When they returned, the second
donor put his phone in his pocket.
Q showed the public catalog and
one entry cleared for
demonstration. The donor asked
how many lives the archive
expected to transform. Mariela
asked who would answer requests
on a day when Lucía was ill.
Lucía had budgeted equipment
and space. The hours in the next
column were all volunteered.
Mariela tapped it with the pencil.
“That isn't free. Who is paying for
it now?”
Lucía named herself and two
others. They added paid hours and
reduced the number of items
promised for the first month. The
second donor thought the smaller
target would be harder to present.
Mariela said he could present the
larger one if he came on
Thursdays.
Both contributed. Mariela's gift
covered the first block of paid
hours; the other went toward
equipment. Lucía put the receipts
in an envelope with the amended
budget. Q left at the time he had
given them.
A worse problem followed. The
equipment donor wanted a specific
example of the Isthmus case. Lucía
supplied a redacted extract under a
confidentiality agreement, but
without obtaining the family's
permission to show that recipient
the passage. The donor forwarded
it to an analyst. A clause quoted
from the family's disputed lease
identified the parcel to the
consortium reviewing the extract.
The family received a letter asking
whether it had authorized the
allegations. Lucía had intended a
private illustration for funding.
She had sent a family's case into a
chain it had not chosen.
She called the family first. She had
prepared an explanation of the
agreement the donor had broken.
Before she reached it, they asked
why she had sent him their passage
at all.
“I didn't ask you. I should have,”
she said.
They asked who else had it. She
could name the donor and analyst;
she did not know whether it had
gone farther. Their lawyer asked
her to find out and keep the
replies. The family wanted the
extract withdrawn, not the
evidence of where she had sent it
destroyed.

Q sat beside her afterward while
they made the recipient list. Lucía
dictated the first request, stopped,
and asked him to read it back. He
read it as it stood. She cut the
explanation of what she had
intended and kept the question
about further recipients. The
requests went out separately; the
unanswered ones remained on the
list.
“They don't want this used as an
example of what we learned,” she
said.
“Then it won't go in a funding
report.”
The account in these pages is
limited to the disclosure the
participants later permitted. The
disputed testimony does not
appear here. A reader may dislike
the gap; the family had already
borne enough of the expense of
making a story persuasive.
More people came with recipes,
recordings, legal notices, and
boxes of objects whose importance
had survived the loss of their
original packaging. Lucía and the
keepers recorded what each
depositor wanted done. Some
wanted publication, some a closed
deposit, some help retrieving
another copy. Conflicting claims
were marked for review rather
than settled by the confidence of
the person at the keyboard.
A journalist asked Q to identify the
cases most likely to change
opinion. He offered to discuss the
archive's public process. The
journalist wanted a face. Lucía
gave her contacts for participants
who had chosen to speak and
refused others. The resulting
article called the archive
uncooperative and used a
photograph of Lucía taken through
the window.
Q asked whether she wanted him
to help prepare a correction
request. She wanted the inaccurate
description challenged, and advice
on the photograph's use. He
compared the published
statements with the exchange they
could document. One paragraph
was corrected. The image
remained while the separate
complaint continued.
Their server arrived in a ventilated
cabinet built by one of the
volunteers. The battery and power
equipment stood separately, where
they could be maintained without
heating the stored papers. The
keepers established access
accounts, a backup routine, and a
way to keep disputed items closed.

“Keep both?”
“As long as yours doesn't reduce
the amount.”
They kept both. The list included a
revised scene, a joke, and a pause
before an answer. The pause
occupied most of the ensuing
discussion. Rebeca performed the
line with and without it. Even the
printer stopped long enough to
improve the second version,
although no one proposed
including the printer in the claim.
Efraín used two surname forms in
different parts of his family. He did
not want the workshop to launch a
correction on his behalf. Q asked
whether he wanted both recorded
privately or no new entry at all. He
wanted a note for his own papers
explaining the sources, without an
application being sent to an office.
Q prepared it and returned the
copies to him.
On the third Thursday, a registry
official attended to explain what
her office could handle and which
cases needed a different
procedure. Her name was Paula.
She had also brought a list of
common reasons requests were
returned. Lucía asked her to
distinguish missing information
from information her office simply
preferred in another format.
Paula struck out two requirements
on the workshop's sample
checklist. They had come from a
form for a different procedure. She
would not promise a single rule for
every dispute or waive
documentation she was required to
verify. The conversation became
less comfortable when they
reached the cases still going
nowhere after all the requirements
had been met.
“Those are the ones we need
someone to follow,” Ofelia said.
Paula agreed to supply a contact
and the reference for each return.
She did not agree to decide every
case in the room. Q entered the
promised follow-up and asked
when they should check if no
answer came. The appointment
made her less abstract and the
workload no smaller.
The register did not promise to
return names as if they were
missing objects. It recorded the
source, the discrepancy, the
requested action, the person
entitled to receive an answer, and
the agreed access. A number
distinguished cases; a number did
not replace a name. Disagreement
could remain visible without being
published to every institution that
might find it convenient.

Who Refused a Caption

supermarket envelope. She had

emergency ward. She sat down,
put the envelope on the table and
loosened one shoe with the other
foot.

a bed. Her sister's face was turned
away. They had agreed to a limited
newspaper image during a
public-health emergency, with the
patient's identifying details
concealed. The accompanying
story supplied a birthplace,
children, and a representative
courage that did not correspond to
the account they had given.

reuse and leave the print
somewhere safe for a month while
deciding what else to do. Her sister
had authorized her to handle that

versions and the release could be
compared; the private medical

“We can identify which copy
contains it and request restriction

retrieve copies from everyone who
has already received them.”

the request.”

caption explaining that she refused

Lucía asked whether Alma wanted

The delay belongs to the account as

A journalist later contacted the

“That is the first question I'd
want,” Alma said.
“Would you like to send that
back?” Q asked.
She did. The journalist revised the
questions, but Alma decided not to
take the interview. An article
subsequently described her refusal
as a form of public courage. It used
the newspaper's earlier material,
not the archive's deposited print or
the private account of the comb.
Lucía retained the public article
with the correspondence
concerning its use. Alma's
envelope stayed closed. Keeping a
record of a disputed publication
did not authorize them to make the
underlying image more available in
order to explain why she objected.
On the thirty-first day Alma
returned. The deposit had
remained closed after its review
date. She collected the photograph
and signed the item receipt. She
left the comb receipt under a new
agreement permitting her to
retrieve it and no public display.
“The comb was cheap,” she said. “I
will remember buying it as if it cost
everything.”
Q checked that the printed price
was still legible. “Then keep this.
We can at least prevent the comb
from getting more expensive every
time you tell it.”
“Not less important.”
“No. I'm only disputing the price.”
The later court file would include
the public article and the deposit's
handling record, subject to their
own limits. It would not thereby
acquire an original photograph the
archive no longer held. The ease
with which a description travelled
into an exhibit would still be part
of the dispute.
Three years later Alma returned
with another comb receipt. The
prices had changed. Her sister was
waiting outside and wanted to
know why buying a comb now
required a visit to an archive. Alma
said it did not and took her time
comparing them anyway.
